Consult Summary:
- Mary Jo, a 45-year-old active runner training for a marathon, presents with ~2 weeks of right anterior/anterolateral knee pain with clicking provoked by running and knee flexion/extension; clinician suspects overuse patellofemoral or related mechanical knee pathology and arranged physio referral and prescription for a stronger oral anti-inflammatory.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Right knee pain with audible/subjective clicking, worse with running and with repeated flexion → extension (noticed during abs exercises and gym work).
  - Reduced running tolerance — pain typically begins ~20 minutes into a run (~2.5–3 miles).
  - Transient right toe tingling once after a run.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Symptoms began approximately 2 weeks ago after increasing running mileage as part of marathon training (longer runs started ~1 month ago).
  - Initial mild swelling after first long run resolved with ice; currently no persistent swelling and not painful at rest most of the time.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Aggravated by running and movements requiring knee extension from flexion.
  - Improved with rest and ice.
  - Patient has been using over-the-counter NSAIDs (ibuprofen) intermittently.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - One transient episode of tingling in right toes after a run; no persistent numbness.
  - No fever, redness, warmth, or systemic illness reported.
  - No locking, instability/giving way, or difficulty walking or using stairs.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No current swelling, no locking of the knee, no problems with walking/stairs, no calf pain, no change in skin color or temperature of lower limb.

Past Medical History:
- Generally well; no chronic joint disease reported.
- Surgical history: LASIK for far-sightedness.
- Prior notable events: Emergency visit in the past for suspected kidney stone/UTI (required ED care; details not documented).
- Prior knee trauma: Fall while playing ice hockey months ago causing a large bruise (no documented fracture or surgical repair).

Medications:
- Reported current/occasional medications:
  - Ibuprofen — patient reports occasional use, "400 mg max" (dose/route/frequency as used by patient; prescription details not documented).
  - Aleve (patient named; likely naproxen) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Vitamin D — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Melatonin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Xanax (occasional use) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- New treatment plan: Clinician stated they would send a "slightly stronger anti-inflammatory" prescription to the pharmacy (medication name and dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies:
  - Not documented in transcript.

Social History:
- Lives in London.
- Recreational/athletic:
  - Active runner training for a marathon (recently increased mileage).
  - Plays ice hockey.
- Substance use:
  - Occasional cannabis use ("smokes a joint").
  - No tobacco or alcohol use documented.
- Occupation: Not recorded.
- Financial or lifestyle constraints: Not recorded.

Family History:
- Not documented / no relevant family history of rheumatologic disease mentioned.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings (from history / video consultation):
  - Full active range of motion — able to fully straighten and fully flex the knee.
  - No current swelling or warmth reported on exam.
  - No locking, no giving way/instability reported.
  - No difficulty walking or using stairs.
- If formal in-person exam performed later, findings could be updated.

Investigations:
- No imaging, labs, or formal investigations reported or performed during this consultation.
- Planned/referral:
  - Referral to physiotherapy arranged.
  - Possible imaging (e.g., knee imaging) to be considered if symptoms persist or clinical exam suggests intra-articular pathology.
  - Prescription for a stronger oral anti-inflammatory to be sent to pharmacy (details not documented).

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Overuse-related mechanical knee pain, most consistent with patellofemoral pain syndrome / patellar maltracking (runner's knee), in the context of increased running mileage; other considerations include IT band-related lateral tendinopathy and possible meniscal/cartilage injury related to prior trauma.
- DDx Integration (brief):
  - 1) Patellofemoral pain syndrome / patellar maltracking — HIGH likelihood.
    - Supporting: Onset after increased mileage, activity-related anterior knee pain starting after ~20 minutes running, clicking with flexion/extension, transient swelling improving with ice.
    - Opposing: Patient describes pain sometimes more to the right rather than purely central; limited video exam without observed patellar crepitus.
  - 2) Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome — MEDIUM likelihood.
    - Supporting: Running-related pain that begins partway into runs and lateral component to pain.
    - Opposing: No focal lateral point tenderness documented; clicking favors intra-articular or patellar-tracking causes.
  - 3) Meniscal/cartilage injury (post-traumatic) — MEDIUM likelihood.
    - Supporting: Prior ice-hockey fall months earlier and intermittent clicking with motion.
    - Opposing: No locking, persistent swelling, or focal joint-line tenderness recorded on consultation.
- Conflict noted between transcript and DDx: None significant; DDx aligns with transcript history and clinician impressions.

Issue 1: Right knee pain with clicking — suspected patellofemoral/overuse mechanical problem
- Assessment:
  - Most likely patellofemoral overload / maltracking (runner's knee) related to recent increase in running mileage.
- Plan:
  - Conservative management: Continue ice therapy as patient has been doing.
  - Activity modification: Reduce running intensity/mileage; avoid running through pain; pause long runs if pain requires stopping.
  - Analgesia: Continue OTC NSAIDs as needed; clinician to send prescription for a stronger oral anti-inflammatory (medication name/dose/route/frequency not documented). Advice: do not take the new prescription concurrently with ibuprofen (per clinician) and take with food.
  - Referral: Physiotherapy referral arranged for formal assessment and supervised rehabilitation.
  - Escalation: If symptoms do not improve with physiotherapy and conservative care, consider imaging (e.g., knee X-ray/MRI) and orthopedic review.
  - Safety netting: Return urgently/seek immediate care if persistent/new swelling, increasing warmth/redness, fever, inability to bend/straighten the knee, or acute deterioration.

Issue 2: One-time transient right toe tingling after exertion
- Assessment:
  - Likely transient exertional nerve irritation or neurapraxia (e.g., compression from footwear or transient swelling) given single episode and resolution.
- Plan:
  - Monitor for recurrence or progression (numbness, persistent paresthesia, motor weakness).
  - If tingling recurs or becomes persistent, re-evaluate in clinic and consider neurological exam and further testing.

Issue 3: Prior knee trauma (ice-hockey fall months ago) — possible underlying cartilage/meniscal contribution
- Assessment:
  - Prior blunt trauma could predispose to meniscal or chondral lesion that may be symptomatic with increased load.
- Plan:
  - Address initially with physiotherapy and activity modification.
  - If mechanical symptoms develop (locking/catching) or failure to improve, arrange clinical re-examination and imaging (MRI) and consider orthopedic referral.

General plan items:
- Do not combine prescription anti-inflammatory with current ibuprofen; take prescription with food.
- Physiotherapy referral placed; clinician offered in-clinic appointment sooner if physio wait is too long.
- Provide urgent review instructions for signs of infection, acute joint lock, systemic illness, or rapidly worsening symptoms.
- Pharmacy prescription to be sent (medication name/dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript).

Quality checks:

  - No documented vital signs.
  - No documented medication allergy list.
  - Prescription medication name/dose/route/frequency and exact durations are not documented in the transcript.
  - No formal in-person physical exam findings (document based on patient reporting/video responses rather than palpation).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant; DDx findings were consistent with transcript history.
- Transcript quality:
  - Consultation audio/transcript intelligible; limited ability to perform physical exam via video (patient-reported exam findings used).
